Put the big number (e.g. '$100M+') in the sky note at 0 s and show a truck leaving the strip, so the image matches the claim before the padlocks arrive.

videos.yt_title: How thieves stole $100M+ of AI servers with paperwork
script: A hundred million dollars of AI freight stolen. Thieves mostly use paperwork.
Why now? Overhaul says one AI server rack costs about three million dollars. So a truck is a vault on wheels.
Yes, GPS was spoofed in one big theft. That means feeding the tracker a fake location. The dashboard happily shows a truck that isn't there.
But don't blame the satellites yet. Overhaul says deception, not force, was used in ninety-two percent of high-value tech thefts.
So how does paperwork steal a truck? Start with freight brokers. Think marriage bureau, matching cargo with truckers.
Step one: hack a broker's account and post fake shipments. Real truckers bid on them. The fake loads are bait.
Step two: send trucking companies a malicious link. One click, and thieves own that account, bidding on real shipments.
Imagine mummy's WhatsApp gets hijacked. 'Give dad's suits to my friend.' The dhobi isn't dumb. The account was right.
And the pickup? Sometimes a real driver, hired unknowingly. Sometimes an accomplice with a fake licence.
Force did show up, on two loads. Thieves deliberately rammed security escorts, and the drivers kept going.
Even then, Scott Cornell of SPG Cargo and Logistics tied both to verification failures. Those drivers 'weren't properly vetted'.
So the weak spot was trust, not the truck. Cornell wants proper driver checks and digital bills of lading, the cargo paperwork, because paper ones let thieves rewrite what's in the box.
If a login can be borrowed, what else do we trust just because it looks like the right account?

fixes.fix: Main seam is Scene 3 → Scene 4. 'Pretend money, but it counts' is followed by 'Microsoft's claim: half the cost, even a third.' Half the cost of what, and compared with whom? A new viewer doesn't know yet that the AI is being compared with doctors' test spending, because the doctors only show up in Scene 9. So the claim arrives as a stray fact, and the 'Remember that' callback in Scene 14 builds on it. The viewer needs to hear that the comparison is with what the doctors ordered on the same cases. Two places where the screen and the voice don't match: (a) at 1 s, WHAT DID IT WIN? is already sliding in while the voice says 'Microsoft's AI beat', and BEAT GENERALISTS / 0 REAL PATIENTS never show up in the 1 s or 4 s frames; (b) at 97 s the sky shows MEANT TO AUGMENT while the voice is still on 'clinical testing is still required', and at 100 s ('Microsoft says no') the sky is empty. Re-time both sky-note tracks to their spoken cue words. The Scene 16 → 17 seam is covered under ending.

Scene 9 is the payoff of the 'beat doctors' hook, but neither 83.2% nor 36.1% can be seen at 58 s ('point two percent') or at 61 s. The exam hall is three identical icon boxes, and the generalists are drawn as a plain 'box'. Write AI 83.2% and GENERALISTS 36.1% large over their desks on the spoken words, and draw the generalists as people. Scenes 3, 7, 9, 11, 14 and 17 all use the same three-box node row, which reads as a diagram slide. Give at least Scenes 9 and 11 real desks with score bars that rise and sag. The Scene 3 price tags can't be seen at 22–25 s either. Also fix the NOT STEP BY STEP heading, which sits on top of the MAIN COMPLAINT layer label at 16 s and 19 s.

Scene 11 crams three beats into one sentence: the stat (about 22%), the multiplier (nearly 4×) and the reframe ('same AI, different yardstick'). The reframe is the key idea before the twist, and it gets rushed. Split it into two lines with a short beat after 'nearly four times'. To pay for the time, cut Scene 7 (anchoring) down to one clause inside Scene 5. That also shortens the 34–52 s stretch of internal mechanics, so the test result arrives sooner.

On the end card, the burned-in caption is still showing 'OR COMPANY?' from Scene 17 instead of the follow line. The cover title 'A MOCK TEST?' runs past both edges, 'NO PATIENTS' and the art are only half drawn, and every frame from 109 s on is identical. Clear the caption band at the scene cut, caption the follow line, and fit the title inside the safe area. Also check whether the last ~3 s of the render are frozen.

Scene 17 states a fact ('Still unsettled: … who's responsible?') but has no source and shows no credit. Add a source for the unresolved-liability point (for example a news or legal analysis of AI diagnostic liability) and show the credit on screen. Otherwise, present it clearly as the narrator's own question rather than a reported fact.

The cliffhanger brings in liability for the first time in the last scene. Nothing earlier raises the question of who is responsible, so it feels tacked on. Either set it up earlier (for example in Scene 16: 'and when it does reach a patient and gets one wrong…'), or tie the cliffhanger to the opening image with the street's shut doors. For example: when one of those doors finally opens to it, who answers if it's wrong? Then the question reads as the next step of this story and not a new topic.

videos.yt_title: Microsoft's AI Beat Doctors on Hard Test Cases. Wait, What?
script: Microsoft's AI beat generalist doctors. It's never met a patient.
So what did it actually win?
It's called D.X.O. Early draft in twenty twenty-five, now published in Science. But the test is strange.
Earlier AI tests weren't step by step. They handed over the whole question paper.
D.X.O. gets one line. Just the patient's main complaint.
Picture a doctor hearing only that, then choosing every question, every test.
And every test has a price tag. Pretend money, but it counts.
Microsoft's claim: half the cost, even a third. Remember that.
Inside, it's not one AI. It's a whole panel.
One suggests diagnoses, one picks tests, one challenges everyone, one watches the bill.
Basically a society committee. Except this one actually checks the accounts.
Why argue? Authors suggest it may stop the AI clinging to its first guess. That's called anchoring.
How was it tested? Three hundred and four hard cases from the New England Journal of Medicine.
In the Science version, Gizmodo reports, it scored eighty-three point two percent.
Generalist doctors, with reference materials, got thirty-six point one percent.
That's more than twice. Cue the headlines.
Take away their reference materials: about twenty-two percent. Now it's nearly four times. Same AI, different yardstick.
Look at who it beat: generalists, without their team, on rare, tough cases. Not a real clinic.
Not specialists. The researchers themselves expect the gap to narrow against experts.
Remember the half-cost claim? Estimated, on simulated cases. Not real hospital bills.
So what did it actually win? First rank in a very hard mock test.
No real patient yet. Microsoft's AI chief says clinical testing is still required.
Replace doctors? Microsoft says no. It's meant to augment them.
Still unsettled: if an AI-assisted diagnosis is wrong, who's responsible? Doctor, hospital, or company?

videos.yt_title: Black October: Why Sites Went Offline to Patch PHP
script: Parts of the internet pulled their shutters down. On purpose.
So who did more damage: hackers, or shutters?
Bits of Wikipedia's parent, Wikimedia. All of Finland's government sites. And… four-chan.
The cause? A hole in PHP, the cook that makes each page fresh when you open it.
Nearly seven in ten sites we can check? Cooked in PHP. The internet's dal-chawal.
But two bugs, nicknamed PHP-to-Shell, opened the kitchen's back door. No login needed.
Imagine a stranger walks in and cooks whatever he wants. That's "running code on a server."
Rated nine point two out of ten. And that door? Fourteen years old.
Back in twenty twenty-four, a PHP developer spotted one of these flaws.
The team couldn't agree on a fix. Very society WhatsApp group.
This August, researchers at Calif and Wiz found both bugs. With AI.
Chainguard's CEO says they just asked an AI to "find bad vulnerabilities in PHP."
Then the news leaked. A day before the fix.
Forty-five minutes after the announcement, Cloudflare saw tens of thousands of attempts. Millions by the twenty-second.
Agencies like the N.S.A. said: patch now, or go offline. So, shutters down.
Nobody could open those sites. Not hackers. Not you.
And as of the twenty-third? Not one confirmed break-in.
Unconfirmed isn't none. But Sophos says attackers seem to be struggling.
So who did more damage? So far, the shutters. The attackers? Still knocking.
That same day, Censys counted over thirty-four million PHP services still on vulnerable versions.
Run a PHP site? Update PHP itself. Too old? Ask your host. Tonight.
When AI helps find the next hole, who's faster: finders, or fixers?
Follow, and tomorrow you learn the next one.

slides_text.heading: This AI got 83.2% on hard cases. Generalist doctors got 36.1%.
slides_text.body: Microsoft's numbers, on rare test cases, not real patients. Here's the catch.

slides_text.heading: It never sees the full case file

cards.caption:
An AI scored 83.2% on hard medical cases. Generalist doctors got 36.1%. But there's a catch.
Microsoft's MAI-DxO starts with only a chief complaint, then picks which questions to ask and which tests to order. Every step carries a virtual price tag.
Inside, AI agents play roles like proposing diagnoses, challenging assumptions and weighing costs. These are company-reported results on rare test cases, not real patients, and clinical testing is still needed.
Could cheaper, smarter testing matter in India? That's our inference, not a plan.

cards.title: Black October: the PHP hole

slides_text.heading: A 14-year-old hole sat under nearly 7 in 10 websites
slides_text.body: An AI-assisted search found it. Then parts of the internet switched themselves off.

slides_text.heading: PHP builds the page each time you open a site
slides_text.body: of sites with a known server language use PHP, as of 24 October 2026. WordPress runs on it.

slides_text.heading: Two bugs let a stranger run code on the server
slides_text.body: Nicknamed PHP2Shell. No login needed. Both are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity. They go back to PHP 5.4, from 2012.

slides_text.heading: Researchers found them with AI, in August
slides_text.body: Humans used AI tools. Chainguard's CEO says they typed 'find bad vulnerabilities in PHP' into a frontier AI model.

slides_text.heading: Then the tries exploded: millions by 22 October
slides_text.body: Cloudflare saw these attempts, not successful attacks. The news had leaked a day early, on 20 October.

slides_text.heading: So some sites chose to go dark to patch
The twist: no confirmed break-in so far
slides_text.body: As of 23 October. That isn't the same as none. Shutdowns were the visible damage. Is that the new normal?

cards.caption:
A 14-year-old hole sat under nearly 7 in 10 websites. AI-assisted search found it.

Two PHP bugs, nicknamed PHP2Shell, let a stranger run code on a server without logging in. Both are rated 9.2 out of 10. Cloudflare saw millions of attempts by 22 October, and some sites went offline on purpose to patch.

As of 23 October, there's no confirmed break-in. That isn't the same as none.

Should shutting down to patch be the new normal? 🤔

lessons.text: Every video must have a proper thumbnail/cover, and its text must hedge exactly like the narration (same qualifiers, no stronger claim than the voiceover makes).

Keep a single ending beat after the payoff (one closing question or one practical takeaway, not both stacked) and a short tail (about 10 s or less); fold any extra stat into the scene before. Never write a follow call to action: the pipeline's end card adds it.

Never leave a frame near-empty while the narrator is speaking: every key phrase (stat, rating, quote intro) needs its visual on screen from the first frame and held until the line ends. Check keyframes at each narration cue for blank pages.
When revising a script, keep the first draft's voice, jokes and rhythm; fix only what the notes name. In a blind test the owner preferred the first draft over the final revised one.

Make the script flow for a first-time viewer: every part should lead into the next, and when the story moves on, the viewer should know what is being answered now and why. Use whatever fits the moment (a spoken question, a 'but' or 'so', a callback, a quick bridge) and vary it; never just jump to an answer the viewer wasn't set up for.

Time each reveal visual to its narration cue and in the storyboard order. Show the big number, the object or the quote card on the cue word, hold it until the line ends, and don't show later text early.
After the payoff, run one ending beat only. Fold any extra stat into the preceding action scene rather than adding another closing scene, and keep the tail after the payoff short (about 10s or less).

Keep the picture in step with the voice: headings, labels and on-screen questions should match what is being said at that moment and help the viewer follow where the story is going, not introduce a question or point the narration never makes.

Give the headline stat its own dominant visual: show the big number large on screen on the cue word and keep both compared numbers visible together until the line ends, with props that make the setting readable (e.g. two labelled desks with score sheets). Never leave the key number tiny or absent.

Change the on-screen note or visual on every clause of the narration, and don't let one scene's overlay fall back to a single note. Check that no stretch over 2.5 s repeats the same frame, especially the opening seconds, and that no blank frame sits before the end card.

Put sound accents on the biggest moments: every riser must resolve into an impact on the key number or reveal, and thin out whooshes/pops in busy scenes (no more than about one SFX per 2 s) so the peak stands out.
Give each scene only one new fact, and when the video runs longer, add a bridge line that links the previous fact to the next instead of adding another fact.
Leave about 0.5 s of clean silence directly before any twist or big reveal impact, with no whoosh, tick or other effect in that gap, so the peak lands on air.

Name the subject in the first spoken line: the opening sentence must say who or what it is ("An AI just beat generalist doctors..."), never open on a bare pronoun like "It" whose referent is shown or named only later.

Before the final cut, check every number, venue and method claim in the script against the exact source version it cites (journal vs preprint), and make the end card and kicker stats identical to the script's stats; add the journal DOI to the source list whenever the script names a journal.
Keep every spoken number and every quoted phrase whole inside one caption chunk (e.g. "304 HARD CASES", "CUE EVERY 'AI'"); split captions only at phrase boundaries that never break a number or quote.

Before any later line corrects, answers or follows up on a claim (e.g. "And the savings?", "if it orders cheaper tests"), state that claim in plain words in an earlier scene. The viewer must have heard the claim before the rebuttal names it.

Before final cut, check that no two on-screen labels overlap and no stamp or sticker covers a label that names a key subject. Move or shrink the overlay until every label reads clearly on the frame where it appears.

Every object the narration names as a running thread (money, bills, score sheets, price tags) must be drawn on screen in each scene that mentions it. If a scene says a bill or cost, show the bill prop in that scene; never rely on captions alone to carry it.

Re-hook the viewer at least every 10 seconds of narration: restate the open question, tease the next reveal, or name the stake again. No stretch of spoken narration may run longer than about 10 s without a hook line.

Vary the diagram layout from scene to scene: never reuse the same node row or three-box template in more than two scenes. When a scene is about people (doctors, generalists, patients), draw them as people at desks with score bars that rise and sag, not as identical boxes or icons.

Every factual claim about law, liability or an unresolved issue must name its source, and that source credit must appear on screen in that scene. If no source is cited, phrase the point explicitly as the narrator's own question, never as a reported fact.

Write every line as natural spoken sentences with a subject and a verb, the way a friend talks. Never use headline fragments ('Its fix?', 'A launch asterisk:', 'Half the fare tempts.'). Each script needs at least one joke that carries a fact, not only a label.

When the narration names a metaphor that stands for a running value (a meter, a bill, a tally), draw that one prop on screen the first time it is named, make it tick or change with the value, and reuse the same prop when the narration calls back to it. Do not swap in a different graphic for the same idea.

Keep every animated character, label and overlay above the caption-band safe line in every frame. Before final cut, scrub each scene where moving art enters the bottom of the frame and confirm nothing overlaps the subtitle text.

Introduce every technical term (token, weights, index, API) in a plain spoken sentence before the first line that uses it or prices it. The viewer should hear the word explained before any question about it or any number attached to it.

Limit background-music changes to about one per major section (about three per video), and make the payoff scene's music energy the highest in the video, with a riser into the key line and an impact on the revealed number.

Give the central concept at least as much narration time as any side detour that supports the story. Before final cut, time both; if a detour runs longer, cut it to one line and fold it into the adjacent scene.

When the story takes a side topic (a price, a stat, a detour), say out loud in its first line how it bears on the open question, and return to that question in its last line before the story moves on. The viewer should never hear a fact that has no link to the loop.
End on one concrete action the viewer can take that names the test that would settle the open question (who must run it, on what, and when), instead of a vague 'wait and see' line.
When the narration announces a twist or reversal, draw the twist as an action on screen (a layer dropped into the stack, a label swapped, a number flipped), not only as a suspicious reaction face.

When you apply a statistic to a new case, keep the population it measured in the same line and do not turn it into a general rule about the new case. For example, a deception rate from high-value tech thefts cannot be stated as "thieves mostly use paperwork" about a different heist; say "in most high-tech heists, nobody forces anything; they fake the paperwork" and attribute the figure to its source.

Keep every animated number, board or prop inside the left and right frame edges as well as above the caption-band line, and check that the final settled value is fully readable in the last frame of its animation. Scale the board down so the full value fits, not just the first few digits.
When a line introduces a word that implies a purpose or target (bait, decoy, cover, lure), say in that same sentence what it targets, so the next beat can connect to it.
Credit each on-screen figure to the outlet that published that exact number, not an aggregator that repeated it. Name the original outlet on the hook card where the figure first appears.

A quote card or text-only scene must still carry a drawn action that changes on screen during the quote, such as a checklist box ticking or a prop swinging open. Words building up on a blank card do not count as a visual change.

Before final cut, check every on-screen text element for legibility on a phone at 1080 wide: source chips and footnotes at least 34 px, small labels (countdown, counters) at least 28 px, and wordmarks, banners and edge props fully inside the frame, never cut off ('The Daily Habi'). Cut any text that cannot be made that size.

Match the host character's expression to each line's emotion and keep one art style for the character in every scene, including the outro. Use confident for a big claim, a shrug for 'no word yet', neutral or pleased for good news, and hopeful for 'fingers crossed'. Avoid mid-blink frames, flat or alarmed faces on neutral lines, and a different art style.

Pick a graphic that shows the story's real comparison, and say the headline number in plain terms. Do not chart values that can't be compared (input vs output price). Use a big stat with a clear label and the claimant (e.g. '50% cheaper, OpenAI's claim'). Keep the claim wording no stronger than the source, and credit the primary source (filing, wire service, government body), not an aggregator.

Keep the topic graphic on screen beside a smaller host in every scene, including punchlines and bridges; never cut to a full-frame host that hides it. Switch the topic strip at the bridge line, not after it. Colour data by meaning (losses red, revenue blue/neutral).

Keep the opening and wide shots clean: no more than a card plus one strip and caption in the first seconds, no leftover logo cards, no wordmark in the bottom 420 px or cut off, and captions on one line in one box with no strike or underline rule, capped at x 860. Every spoken line needs a caption (no gaps in the PIP shots). Use the same host art in every scene, with no black filler frame at the end.

Tie the outro to the show's running thread by calling back to at least two segments, and end with the sign-off line. Write a handoff line that links to the next segment, never a throwaway like 'Okay gamers, your turn'. Don't repeat in the first segment a phrase the hook already said. Check each claim's timing and count (a June listing week is not 'today'; 'one chipmaker', not 'chipmakers'). Cut details that aren't in the facts, and keep each segment to 22-28 words.

knowledge.text: Two bugs in PHP, nicknamed PHP2Shell, let an attacker run their own code on a web server without logging in.
Both bugs are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

PHP is the programming language behind 69.3 percent (nearly 7 in 10) of websites whose server-side language is known (W3Techs, 24 October 2026); it builds the page each time you open one, and runs WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.
Affected versions go back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012: the hole existed for about 14 years.
In 2024 a PHP core developer noticed the memory error behind one of the bugs during an audit; it was left unfixed because the team couldn't agree on a fix and no one had shown an exploit.

Researchers found the bugs in August 2026 using AI: Ryan Austin of the security firm Calif with an OpenAI model in OpenAI's 'Patch the Planet' project, and Wiz researchers independently with Google and OpenAI models.
Chainguard's CEO, Dan Lorenc, says his company found the same bugs by typing 'find bad vulnerabilities in PHP' into a frontier AI model.
OpenAI said: 'To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.'
News of the bugs leaked a day early, on 20 October; the fixes came out on 21 October 2026.
Amazon's honeypots caught an attempt to exploit the bugs on 17 October, four days before they were made public.

Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince: thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before the announcement; tens of thousands within 45 minutes after; hundreds of thousands within 2 hours; millions by 22 October. These are attempts Cloudflare saw (and blocked for its customers), not successful attacks.

Taken offline to patch, on purpose: several Wikimedia (Wikipedia's parent) services, the Internet Archive briefly, 4chan, all of Finland's public government web services and all French Interior Ministry websites. While they were down, those services were unreachable for everyone.
Censys counted over 34.4 million PHP services still running vulnerable versions on 23 October.
As of 23 October no successful break-in had been confirmed; honeypots saw attempts only. Sophos said attackers appear to be struggling, and one attempt to plant botnet malware was blocked.
The security firm Sansec says the public exploits don't work against a default PHP install; an attack needs specific conditions on the server.
Trail of Bits CEO Dan Guido said his team built a working exploit in one day with AI, but 'knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise.'
Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green: 'the whole Internet is dry tinder.'
The fix: update PHP itself to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 (older versions need a fix from the hosting provider or an upgrade).
Agencies including the NSA, CERT-EU and the UK's NCSC told administrators to patch now or take servers that can't be patched offline.
The name 'Black October' came from social media posts calling those 48 hours the worst in cybersecurity history.

The Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO, also called DxO) is described in a paper titled 'Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models'. A preprint appeared on arXiv in 2025, and the peer-reviewed version was published in Science on Thursday, 22 October 2026.
DxO works sequentially. It starts from a chief complaint and decides which follow-up questions and tests to order, instead of receiving a full patient file at once.

The system simulates a panel of physicians. AI agents take roles such as proposing diagnoses, selecting tests, challenging assumptions and weighing costs. The authors suggest this may reduce cognitive biases such as anchoring.
Gizmodo reports that on complex NEJM cases, DxO reached 83.2% accuracy. Generalist physicians with reference materials reached 36.1%.
When generalist physicians were denied reference materials, their accuracy dropped to roughly 22%, which Gizmodo says makes DxO nearly four times as accurate.
On emergency department admissions, DxO scored 80.3% against 46.8% for generalists, a narrower margin.
The strongest results came with OpenAI's GPT-5. Testing with GPT-5.5 showed further improvement.
Microsoft says DxO works at half or even one third of the cost. The savings are based on estimated costs in simulated cases, not real medical bills.

The benchmark, SDBench, turns 304 diagnostically challenging New England Journal of Medicine case records into step-by-step diagnostic encounters. Earlier benchmarks did not test diagnosis sequentially.

In the original June 2025 announcement, 21 US and UK physicians worked alone without textbooks, colleagues or AI tools. They averaged 20% accuracy, against 85.5% for MAI-DxO, as reported by the company.
Each test or question carried a virtual cost, so researchers could measure cost efficiency alongside accuracy. Users can set cost constraints.
The researchers said they would expect the performance gap to narrow if DxO were compared with expert specialists instead of generalists.
Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says clinical testing is still required before real-world deployment.

Testing is planned at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston within about two months, per Dr. Dominic King. A separate search summary says this will test triage of patients in emergency department waiting rooms.
Microsoft says the tool is meant to augment physicians, not replace them.
A 2025 study found doctors who relied on AI for colonoscopy cancer-risk detection performed worse once the AI was removed, per Gizmodo.
NBC News reported thieves have stolen more than $100 million in data center freight since June 2026.
Thieves hack freight brokers' accounts, post fake shipments to attract real bids, and send malicious links to trucking companies; once clicked, they take over accounts and bid on real shipments.
Real drivers are sometimes hired unknowingly to pick up cargo; in other cases fake driver's licenses place accomplices as drivers.
In one of the largest thefts, GPS tracking coordinates were spoofed to avoid digital monitoring.
Targets include servers, fiber-optic cables, memory chips, copper wire and bitcoin mining machines.
In two of the largest thefts, nothing was recovered, and off-duty police officers hired as escorts were targeted in hit-and-run incidents.
A Los Angeles County Sheriff's sergeant told NBC this is how most of these thefts are now carried out, unlike earlier mostly opportunistic highway thefts.
In Los Angeles County, police recovered data center cooling equipment bound for Deepcool AI, mixed with nicotine pouches, TVs and cosmetics.
Cook County Sheriff's Office estimated two stolen loads held about $300,000 in copper wire and about $1 million in data center power equipment.
Scott Cornell of SPG Cargo & Logistics confirmed $110.6 million in known reported data center and high-tech cargo thefts since June 3; individual cases ranged from $2 million to $38 million.

Thieves deliberately crashed into security escorts on two high-value tech loads and the drivers kept going; Cornell linked both to carrier verification failures and said drivers 'weren't properly vetted'.
Cornell estimated six or seven of every 10 stolen US loads now leave the country.
Overhaul says cargo thieves stole more than $150 million in AI equipment in 2026, and thefts of data center equipment, chips and computing components rose 34% since 2024.
A flagship AI server rack costs about $3 million, per Overhaul, so one truckload can hold eight figures in value.
Overhaul says deception (not force) was used in 92% of thefts involving high-value technology shipments, a shift 'from force to fraud'.
Arizona passed a law in July 2026 creating a statewide cargo theft task force and enhanced sentences for fraud-based theft; California, Michigan and Tennessee also passed cargo theft laws in 2026.
Cornell recommends secure digital bills of lading and thorough carrier and driver checks, noting paper bills of lading let thieves alter product descriptions.

hooks.text: Wikipedia's parent switched services off. So far, nobody had broken in.
The internet just switched off the lights to change a lock.
How do you steal a three-million-dollar server rack without a crowbar?
Millions of attempts. Zero confirmed break-ins. So far.
Why did Finland switch off its own government websites?
'Black October' sounds like the hackers won. So far, they haven't.
'AI beat doctors' has a catch, and it's which doctors.
It beat generalist doctors. It hasn't met a single real patient.
What if an AI had to pay for every test it ordered?
Finland switched off every public government website. As a precaution.
Imagine seven of ten houses on your street sharing one lock.
Chainguard's CEO says one sentence typed into an AI found this.
You'd think hackers took these sites down. They didn't.
Microsoft's new AI doctor pays for every test. In pretend money.
Picture a family WhatsApp group where every uncle is a doctor.
An AI gets one complaint. Now it has to ask the right questions.
You think they just spoofed GPS. That's the small part.
Truck thieves aren't smashing windows anymore. They're sending links.
A fourteen-year-old hole in PHP. Found by people using AI.
In twenty twenty-four, someone spotted this bug. It stayed unfixed.
Fourteen years old. Tens of thousands of attempts in forty-five minutes.
On Thursday, Science published an AI that argues with itself.
How do you even check if an AI is a good doctor?
That 'urgent' work link you ignore? It's how this heist starts.

analogies.text: Parts of the internet pulled their shutters down. On purpose.
The cause? A hole in PHP, the cook that makes each page fresh when you open it.
Nearly seven in ten sites we can check? Cooked in PHP. The internet's dal-chawal.
But two bugs, nicknamed PHP-to-Shell, opened the kitchen's back door. No login needed.
Imagine a stranger walks in and cooks whatever he wants. That's "running code on a server."
The team couldn't agree on a fix. Very society WhatsApp group.
Earlier AI tests weren't step by step. They handed over the whole question paper.
Basically a society committee. Except this one actually checks the accounts.
So what did it actually win? First rank in a very hard mock test.
Why now? Overhaul says one AI server rack costs about three million dollars. So a truck is a vault on wheels.
So how does paperwork steal a truck? Start with freight brokers. Think marriage bureau, matching cargo with truckers.
Imagine mummy's WhatsApp gets hijacked. 'Give dad's suits to my friend.' The dhobi isn't dumb. The account was right.

scenes.text: A paper street of four named sites at dusk. Rolling shutters slam down door after door while nobody is outside; then a cartoon figure tagged HACKER rattles the closed shutters.
scenes.why: The hook is about choosing to close, not being broken into. Shopkeepers pulling shutters before a storm says 'on purpose' in a second and builds the street we return to.

scenes.text: A desk of index cards, one per site that closed, each getting an OFFLINE rubber stamp; the last one lands the joke.
scenes.why: A list ending on a punchline: each stamp is a beat, and the held last stamp lands 'four-chan'.

scenes.text: A paper restaurant: the viewer's phone on the left, the PHP kitchen on the right. An order flies in, the kitchen steams, a fresh page comes back.
scenes.why: Before the hole means anything, the viewer must see what PHP does: a cook making your page fresh when you open it.

scenes.text: Words as food: the stat slams in over sun rays, gets circled, then a DAL-CHAWAL stamp thumps down like a steel plate.
scenes.why: 'Nearly 7 in 10' is dry; dal-chawal makes it feel ordinary and everywhere, which is why one hole matters.

scenes.text: The same kitchen, now facing a STRANGER. The kitchen's back door swings open, a red slip flies in, the kitchen turns red and a terminal types what the stranger cooks.
scenes.why: A callback to the kitchen we just learned. 'Running code on a server' becomes a stranger at the stove with no login, which anyone can picture.

scenes.text: A railway split-flap board: the severity rating slams in, the board rolls from 2012 to 2026, then a birthday cake with 14 candles pops up.
scenes.why: Two numbers, two things: 9.2 lands as a caption, and the door's age becomes a board rolling through the years and a cake you can count.

scenes.text: A hand-drawn team chat window labelled re-enactment: the flaw gets posted, typing dots blink, a jumble of contradicting replies types out, and a NO AGREEMENT stamp lands.
scenes.why: 'Couldn't agree on a fix' is abstract. A group chat that argues and decides nothing is the joke, and every viewer has been in that group.

scenes.text: A case-file headline: the finders' names slam in, 'FOUND BOTH BUGS' is written in marker, and a blue WITH AI stamp lands.
scenes.why: The turn is who found the bugs and how. Plain names plus a blue AI stamp set up the finders-versus-fixers question at the end.

scenes.text: A paper quote card: the one plain sentence typed to an AI appears word by word, gets highlighted, and a bug doodle crawls out and stays wiggling to the cut.
scenes.why: The shock is how short the request was. Reading the exact quote shows how easy it was.

scenes.text: A drawn thermometer climbing toward red, with EXPLOIT ATTEMPT alert cards piling up behind it faster at each step.
scenes.why: Leak, then tens of thousands, then millions: the steps climb, so the meter and the card pile-up show the speed without a lonely number.

scenes.text: Callback: the opening street. The agencies' order is written in the sky, windows go dark one by one, shutters slam, and the HACKER figure rattles shutters that won't open. Nobody gets in, not even you.
scenes.why: The script calls back to 'shutters down', so the same street returns and we now know why it closed and who it shut out.

scenes.text: Bare paper in near silence. A zero slams in, 'BREAK-INS' is written under it and circled, and a PLOT TWIST stamp has already landed above.
scenes.why: After the meter boils over, silence makes the zero land. The stamp reads as a twist in under a second.

scenes.text: A sober typed note: 'UNCONFIRMED ≠ NONE' types out, then 'ATTACKERS' drops and 'STRUGGLING' scrambles in red, credited to Sophos.
scenes.why: This is the honest caveat. A plain typed line in a quieter style keeps the twist from overclaiming and credits the source.

scenes.text: The street drops back in. The question returns in the sky, shutters slam on 'the shutters', and the HACKER figure walks the doors still knocking.
scenes.why: The payoff answers the hook on the same street: so far the closed shutters did the damage, and the hackers are still outside knocking.

scenes.text: A quiet split-flap board, like a cricket scoreboard, ticking from 0 up to 34, then 'OVER 34 MILLION' and 'STILL VULNERABLE'.
scenes.why: A sober line after the joke: the count ticks up like a running score that isn't over yet.

scenes.text: A to-do note written straight to the viewer about their own site, line by line, ending on a red TONIGHT stamp.
scenes.why: The viewer's own life: short actions written as a checklist they could follow tonight. No metaphor gets in the way of the instruction.

scenes.text: The street one last time. A small robot tagged AI walks the doors checking each lock, FINDERS and FIXERS sprint to the same door, and a red question mark lands and holds.
scenes.why: The cliffhanger is a race. Reusing the street closes the visual loop and leaves the question open on one hit.

scenes.text: A warm paper street in the viewer's neighbourhood: your clinic, a pharmacy, a hospital tower in the middle and a path lab. Every door is shut and nobody is inside. Big handwritten sky notes follow the voice: the claim, the catch, the question.
scenes.why: The hook needs a real world straight away. The AI 'won' at medicine on a street where it never walked into one clinic. The same street carries the loop, so 'what did it win?' is asked over the same shut doors. Every note starts on a phrase that is spoken and ends on the next one, so the sky never runs ahead of the voice.

scenes.text: Three index cards on a desk: the system, its 2025 preprint and the journal. Only the journal card gets a PUBLISHED stamp.
scenes.why: A quick 'this is real' moment that sets up the two versions of the work: the 2025 preprint and the Science paper. The stamp lands on 'published in Science' and goes only on the Science card, because a preprint is not published. 2025 is shown on its card.

scenes.text: The whole case file as a stack of layers (full history, scans, lab results, exam notes, main complaint) that drops in, then lifts apart to show the whole paper. Then only the top slip, the main complaint, slides out and shakes while the rest dim, and a stamp lands on it.
scenes.why: One continuous move for two linked beats: 'earlier tests handed over the whole paper' becomes the full file laid open, and 'D.X.O. gets one line' becomes the same file collapsing to a single slip. The kicker is on screen from frame one so the page is never empty. The riser ends on the stamp at 'main complaint'.

scenes.text: Your own clinic as a little pipeline: the one-line slip goes to your doctor, who sends questions back and test orders out, and every test sends a yellow bill back.
scenes.why: An order slip goes in and decisions come out, made medical. It puts the viewer's own doctor on screen. Holding the same world for the price-tag line makes the 'pretend money' bill an object, not a number.

scenes.text: A committee table: four AI name cards are dealt in, and each gets an ON PANEL stamp as its job is named.
scenes.why: 'Not one AI' becomes a seated panel with name plates. Each role lands on its own words (suggests diagnoses, picks tests, challenges everyone, watches the bill), so the structure is easy to follow. Sound is thinned so the voice stays on top.

scenes.text: A housing society's stack of account books. For once, the committee pulls out the bills and actually stamps them checked.
scenes.why: The colony committee, except this one does its job. A drawn ledger being checked lands the joke as a picture, with the stamp on 'the accounts' as the punchline.

scenes.text: Two nodes: a red FIRST GUESS slip goes to the ARGUER robot, which bounces it back with 'check again'. 'Anchoring' is named at the end.
scenes.why: This shows why the panel argues: the first guess goes in and gets bounced back instead of being accepted. The kicker labels it as the authors' view (they say it 'may' stop the clinging), and the word 'anchoring' gets its own note when it is spoken.

scenes.text: A railway-style split-flap board rattles from 0 up to 304, the size of the exam, then names the cases and how they were turned into visits.
scenes.why: The number appears as a mechanical count that lands on 304 as it is spoken, and it kicks off the escalation along with the new driving track. The journal is credited in the sub-line, and a second caption turns 'step-by-step visits' into words on the board so the back half of the line has something to see.

scenes.text: An exam hall in three nodes: the AI panel's desk, the 304-case paper in the middle, and the generalists' desk. The paper goes to each desk. The AI desk's score is written large on 'eighty-three point two', then the generalists' score on 'thirty-six point one', and both stay up until the scene ends. The source credit (Science paper, Gizmodo) is in the kicker from frame one.
scenes.why: Both scores sit in one picture, so 'more than twice' is something you can see. Desks and an exam paper are drawn from the first frame, so the page is never empty. Each score is a labelled note (AI: 83.2%, DOCTORS: 36.1%), so a viewer never has to hold a number by ear. The kicker pays off the preprint/Science cards from scene 1. The riser ends on the AI score.

scenes.text: A hype thermometer rushes up while 'AI BEATS DOCTORS!' cartoon headline cards pile up behind it like phone alerts, faster and faster.
scenes.why: This is peak escalation: 'more than twice' climbs, then the headline flood makes the hype visible right before the correction. The cards are plainly cartoon headlines, and the 83.2 vs 36.1 stay on the first step so both numbers are still shown.

scenes.text: The exam hall returns in three nodes: BOOKS, GENERALISTS and AI PANEL. The books are taken away, the generalists' desk drops to about 22%, and the multiplier changes to nearly 4×. The last clause sends a 'who you compare' envelope across.
scenes.why: The previous scene hyped '2×'. This one is the honest correction, built from the same desks so the viewer sees the same people scoring lower, not a new set of numbers. Each figure is a note on its spoken words, and the closing envelope makes 'it depends who you compare' a moving object. Energy stays up because the twist comes next.

scenes.text: The music cuts out. Five plain index cards spell out who it really beat and under what conditions, and each gets a red SMALL PRINT stamp.
scenes.why: The twist lands in near silence with a scratch, and the stamps cool the hype. Each card matches a phrase in the line, in order (generalists, working alone, rare, tough, not a real clinic), so every stamp lands on its word. 'Small print' is a familiar idiom that needs no setup.

scenes.text: The opponent it never faced: a SPECIALISTS slab slides out of a two-slab stack and gets a NOT FACED stamp, with a note giving the narrowing gap as the researchers' own expectation.
scenes.why: 'Not specialists' becomes a physical object: the slab that was never tested. The narrowing gap is shown as the researchers' expectation, not ours, with their name written in the note.

scenes.text: The pipeline comes back: the AI panel works on a simulated case, and the yellow bill that comes back is marked pretend, with the savings an estimate.
scenes.why: This calls back the yellow BILL envelope from the clinic flow, so 'estimated, simulated, not real bills' reads as the same pretend money from earlier.

scenes.text: A report-card moment on a sunburst: the opening question scrambles back, then a red RANK #1 stamp lands, qualified by 'in a MOCK TEST' in blue marker.
scenes.why: This closes the open loop: the callback question resolves into a topper's stamp, and 'mock test' is circled as the honest qualifier. The burst, the scrambling question and the stamp mean the page is never empty. The riser ends on the RANK #1 stamp.

scenes.text: Back on the opening clinic street, quieter now. The doors are still shut. Sky notes follow the voice: no real patient yet, testing still needed, replace doctors? Microsoft: no, meant to augment. The AI robot walks past the shut doors on 'AI chief'.
scenes.why: This world callback to scene 0 grounds the payoff: the same unvisited clinics, now with the AI robot on the street. Each note starts on the phrase it illustrates and ends on the next one, so 'MEANT TO AUGMENT' cannot appear before it is spoken. Four buildings and no zoom, so nothing is cropped.

scenes.text: A three-node lineup: DOCTOR, HOSPITAL and COMPANY. A WRONG CALL slip is passed along the line, then each suspect wobbles in turn as it is named, and the question is left hanging.
scenes.why: The cliffhanger as a lineup with no verdict. The slip travels from company to hospital to doctor, each suspect wobbles on its own spoken word, and nothing is stamped, so the question stays open. Every note and cue is taken from the closing line.

scenes.text: A paper strip of roadside freight depots: AI depot, warehouse, data center, truck yard. They draw on, then every door gets the same padlock. Handwritten notes in the sky follow the voice.
scenes.why: The hook says $100M+ of AI freight was stolen and that the pattern is paperwork. Intact locks on every door show nothing was broken into. The same street returns for the payoff.

scenes.text: A railway-style split-flap board on paper, rolling up to the price of one AI server rack, then calling it a vault on wheels.
scenes.why: The digits roll up to about $3,000,000 on 'Overhaul says', with the source credited on the board. The caption lands on the number, then on the vault line, in spoken order.

scenes.text: A truck tracker sends its real dot to a dispatcher's dashboard. Then a fake signal sneaks in through a back door and the dot lies.
scenes.why: It explains GPS spoofing as a lying dot, a real dot first and then a fake one. It claims only what the script says: one big theft.

scenes.text: A thermometer of force against deception climbs step by step while a few DECEPTION alert cards pile up behind it.
scenes.why: 'Don't blame the satellites yet' turns the story. A climbing meter, with Overhaul credited in the kicker, builds to the 92% stat.

scenes.text: A cartoon matchmaking office. A broker aunty introduces a shipper uncle to a trucker.
scenes.why: The joke explains a freight broker in a second. The broker points and moves on every phrase, so the picture never sits still.

scenes.text: Index cards of fake loads fly in under a hacked-broker heading, and each gets a red BAIT stamp.
scenes.why: Step one is shown as an action. The hacked account posts fake loads and the cards are stamped BAIT, which is the only purpose the script gives them.

scenes.text: Thieves send a link to a trucking firm's phone. One click opens the back door and the firm's account bids on a real load.
scenes.why: A slipped-in note that makes someone obey a stranger is what a malicious link does. The red takeover and the bid keep step two in one picture.

scenes.text: The viewer's own family chat on a hand-drawn phone. 'Mummy' messages the dhobi, but it isn't mummy. Tagged as a re-enactment.
scenes.why: The kicker says it is the same trick at home. It explains the hijacked account in the viewer's own life: a trusted name in a chat is enough to hand over the goods.

scenes.text: Two cartoon drivers side by side at the truck stop. One is cheerful and unaware. The other turns shifty.
scenes.why: The beat names two kinds of collector. Two people, each with an arrow, make the either/or readable at once, and only the accomplice turns suspicious.

scenes.text: Bare paper in near silence. Two index cards, LOAD 1 and LOAD 2, get a red HIT stamp.
scenes.why: This is the twist: the con turns physical. The music cuts and a scratch lands. The stamps act out the ramming on screen.

scenes.text: A quote card with a doodled padlock. Scott Cornell of SPG is credited and 'weren't properly vetted' is swiped with the highlighter.
scenes.why: It bridges force and trust. Even the rammed loads are tied to verification failures, not to the trucks. A real quote is credited to a named person.

scenes.text: Callback: the opening strip of depots, every padlock still shut. The camera pans down to the slab they all stand on, TRUST, and it cracks. Sky notes list Cornell's fixes.
scenes.why: The payoff in one move: the locks held and the shared foundation of trust failed. The notes give Cornell's two fixes and why paper bills are the weak point.

scenes.text: Words on bare paper. A scrambled 'borrowed login' resolves into the question for the viewer, and the last line is circled so the question stays on screen.
scenes.why: The cliffhanger re-points at the video's real trick: an account that looks right. It turns the question onto the viewer's own screen and holds it.
